speakerposition: topic
maintopic: POSSESSION AND USE-ACTION WITH PROVINCES TO CHECK CRIME

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Mr. JOHN BRACKEN (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: POSSESSION AND USE-ACTION WITH PROVINCES TO CHECK CRIME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Minister of Justice. It arises out of several unfortunate occurrences in recent weeks in different parts of Canada, one of them in Ottawa within the last few days.
Has the government made any plans to cooperate with the provincial and municipal authorities in order to check the series of crimes of violence reported from many centres in Canada?
More specifically, has the Minister of Justice considered the advisability of having a conference with the provincial attorneys-general, either at the time of the dominion-provincial conference, or at some other early date, to consider ways and means of coordinating the work of crime prevention and detection?
Has the minister under contemplation any amendments to the criminal code in respect of this problem, and if so, will a bill for that purpose be introduced at this session?
Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Minister of Justice): Mr. Speaker, I received notice of the question only a few moments ago. There is better than plans; there is actual cooperation. I would not attempt in just a few moments to describe all the points of contact and cooperation, but I might indicate some of the highlights which occurred to me when I read the question.
The Royal Canadian Mounted Police is in charge of the provincial police work in six of the nine Canadian provinces-Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta. My information from the commissioner is that during

the war years there have been fewer crimes of violence than there were during the thirties in those provinces, and that there has been no noticeable increase in such crimes since V-E-day.
In the other provinces the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have always stood ready to render to municipal and provincial police authorities all such assistance as is from time to time requested by the attorneys-general of such provinces.
A police bulletin, issued weekly by, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, goes to all provincial forces and to those of incorporated cities and towns throughout Canada. It features all available information considered to be useful in the prevention and detection of crime. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police laboratories, fingerprint records and other records dealing with criminology, their analysts, ballistics experts, bandwriting experts-in a wrord, all their facilities and personnel, are at all times available to all the other police forces in Canada.
In reply to the second question I would say that there are many problems dealing with the administration of justice which it is planned to discuss with the attorneys-general at the dominion-provincial conference, if possible; and if it does not prove to be possible at that time, then as early thereafter as may be convenient to them. This, I may say, is one of those several problems.
My reply to the third question would be that the matter of this outburst of crime and violence has received the attention of the government as well as that of the press throughout the country. On more than one occasion the matter has been discussed by me with my colleagues, and a special committee of the cabinet has been constituted to help me in the preparation of a measure felt to be proper to deal with the situation. It is regarded as one of some urgency. As there is considerable material already before the house, consideration is being given to the question whether or not there will be an order in council, operative only up to such time as legislation can be assented to, or in any event not to be operative after the end of the session if legislation is not assented to; and accompanied at the earliest possible moment by a bill to amend the criminal code in that regard.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: POSSESSION AND USE-ACTION WITH PROVINCES TO CHECK CRIME
speechtext:
May I thank the minister for his full and satisfactory answer.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make an announcement in connection with the negotiations which hon. members will recall have been going on between their employees and the three major meat packing companies of Canada.
Hon. members will recall action was taken in this connection by appointing Mr. Justice Richards a commissioner to assist the parties to come together and discuss their problems. The government also took the unusual action of appointing a controller of the meat packing plants and deputy controllers for various cities where plants are located, and, at the same time, by order in council, required that the plants continue in operation.
No time was lost by the commissioner, Mr. Justice Richards, in getting the parties together, and negotiations have been going on in Winnipeg during the last few days. I might add that representatives of the producers, that is farmers, have sat in during the negotiations.
I am very happy to say that the parties themselves reached a mutually satisfactory agreement at 1.30 a.m. to-day. I am sure hon. members will be glad to hear that negotiations have been satisfactorily concluded. I have not received details of the agreement and of course those affecting wages will have to be finally approved by the appropriate wage boards.
I understand from telephone messages that the main features of the agreement are that the weekly hours are to be reduced from 48 to 45 per week, and that pay will be given for the six legal holidays during the year. Furthermore, it has been agreed upon that a joint 47696-111J
application will be made at once to the appropriate wage boards for an increase of approximately 4j cents per hour.
I feel that we have reason to be well satisfied in regard to the successful outcome of the negotiations, and I also feel hon. members will endorse my expression of appreciation to Mr. Justice Richards and those who have been representing the union and the management of the packing plants, and also those who were good enough to come to the conference as representatives of the farmers.

speakerposition: topic
maintopic: PERMITS TO EX-SERVICE MEN TO GO INTO BUSINESS

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: PERMITS TO EX-SERVICE MEN TO GO INTO BUSINESS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief statement on the issuance of permits to exservicemen to start business.
On Friday last the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) asked me "how much longer returned soldiers are to be refused permits to go into business," apparently suggesting that it was a general policy of the wartime prices and trade board to refuse permits to ex-servicemen. This, of course, is not the case. However, on Tuesday, when he raised the matter again he made it clear that what he had in mind was not so much a general policy but some particular instance, raised in some letter received by an ex-serviceman; so I suggested that he put a question on the order paper. He has not yet disclosed the particular letter to the house. He has, however, disclosed a letter to the press. I have assumed that it w'as the same one and have had the case traced, and am now in a position to make a statement on it without further delay.
Before I tell the house where this particular case stands, it may be useful if I explain the position and policy of the wartime prices board in regard to issuance of licences. Ever since May, 1944, when the whole question was considered by cabinet, the board has in general been issuing licences freely to returned servicemen and others. Flowever, there have been a very few fields where, because of acute shortages of raw material, it would have been pointless to issue licences freely; indeed it wTould have been unfair to existing operators whose supplies had already been drastically reduced, and uneconomical from the point of view of making the best use of available supplies to meet civilian demands. Therefore the board has not been able to grant licences freely to three groups: to industrial sugar users, to users of broom corn, and to certain manufacturers and distributors of textile products. Even here, however, special arrange-

Demobilizations-Army
merits have been made to ensure that exservicemen who immediately before enlistment had owned and operated businesses in these restricted fields, should get not onty their licences but also their appropriate quotas of supplies.
The most recent figures, those for the month of September, show clearly what has been happening. In that month the board issued 3,212 licences to new entrants into business; of these, 710 went to ex-servicemen. Only in nine cases was the board unable to grant licences requested by ex-servicemen; in other words, 98-7 per cent of applications received from ex-servicemen were granted. Further, if those nine cases had been filed within the last week or so they would not have been refused because they were all textile cases and the supply situation is now such that the board expects to be able to grant licences freely within a few weeks.
This brings me back to the case raised by the hon. member for Simcoe North. I find that the application, about which he is apparently concerned, reached the board's licencing division in Ottawa only on Friday, the day that he raised the question in the house, and that the board has dealt with this application in the same way as others being received currently in the textile field. A form letter has gone to this applicant requesting that the board be permitted to hold his application for a short time, because they expect to be able to issue a licence to him within the next few weeks.
I think that the hon, member for Simcoe North may have been misled by the phraseology of the letter which he handed to the press, and I would admit that the terms of the latter are not clear. The official in the board's cotton administration who wrote it was not directly concerned with the issuance or refusal of licences; the matter had been referred to him because he was in a position to advise the applicant about tire position of raw materials in the field he was planning to enter. In. this, as in other cases, the board tried to warn the new entrant of possible troubles ahead; usually such advice is much appreciated. However, as I said before", despite the warning issued, the licence application subsequently came forward to Ottawa in the usual way and it will be approved shortly.

speechtext:
The hon. member for
Nanaimo asked me certain questions with respect to the signal service in the Northwest Territories, to which I have attempted to prepare answers. He asked first whether the wireless stations in the Northwest Territories would be manned in future by the Royal Canadian Corps of Signals. The answer is that it is proposed that the Northwest Territories radio system will continue to be operated by the Royal Canadian Corps of Signals. '
He asked whether these opportunities would be extended to the northwest staging route, which is also an important communication line. My answer is that that is now under consideration. It is probable that the R.C.A.F. will be responsible for the operation of the land line communications facilities on the northwest staging route, but no definite decision as to the final responsibility for operation has yet been taken.
He asked for what amounts were contracts let for the reconstruction of the British Columbia telephone line between Vancouver and Hope, and between Victoria and Campbell river, and also to Port Alberni. My answer is that those contracts were arranged by the Department of Munitions and Supply and the Department of National Defence for Air. When the estimates of these departments are before the committee I think that that information could be made available.
My hon. friend also asked what arrangements had been made for the disposal of the equipment obtained by the Pacific Coast Communications board. That matter is still under consideration, and that same answer I must make
Demobilization-Army

with respect to possible arrangements to continue the service in more remote parts of British Columbia through which telephone lines were constructed for defence purposes, and as to the wireless link between the Charlotte islands and Prince Rupert.

Do I understand that no arrangements have been completed with British Columbia Telephone with respect to the reconstruction of those lines? What will be the disposal of the equipment at the conclusion of hostilities? I was under the impression that arrangements had been made whereby certain equipment would be made available under certain conditions to the B.C. Telephone.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: These questions come within the department of Munitions and Supply or National Defence for Air. Perhaps my hon. friend would put his questions then, or I could bring them to the attention of my colleagues for answer when their estimates are before the committee.
Were not those agreements made by the Department of National Defence for the army?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am advised that the contracts were made by the Department of Munitions and Supply. I am'afraid that I cannot elaborate on that.

I would like to ask a question which relates to each of these items from No. 5 to No. 10. It applies to every one of them. The other day in connection with the naval service the minister said that the accounts were paid by the department. I take it that some of these costs apply to the termination of contracts and for deliveries of stores which were ordered in war and will not be used in war. Can the minister say how much of this item and succeeding items down to No. 10 represents the termination of contract payments, how much represents stores paid for which will have to be destroyed or turned over to War Assets, and how much represents stores which will be useful in the future? Would he at the same time say whether he himself decides on the amount that will have to be paid on the termination of contracts, or is that done in the Department of Munitions and Supply?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
If it is a straight cancellation charge, that amount is taken, up in the estimates of the Department of Munitions and Supply. If the manufacture of the equipment in question is completed and the equipment is delivered to the army, that is included in the item under consideration. It may be that after delivery some of the equipment
[Mr. Abbott. 1
will ultimately be declared surplus and turned over to War Assets. I do not know that I can readily give my hon. friend a break-down of that latter category. I can tell him how much of the estimate covers commitments from the previous year. There have been no new commitments since V-J day. Between V-E day and V-J day there were some new commitments for signal and wireless equipment, because it was then contemplated that we would be carrying on the war against Japan, although I am advised that these commitments were limited. I do not know that I can at this time give definite information as to what portion of the equipment previously ordered and delivered or to .be delivered will ultimately be declared surplus. That whole question is being reviewed by the staff. Obviously we are going to be in a good equipment position, with ample motor vehicles, ample signalling equipment, all the latest and most modern types of equipment for the reserve army and for setting up adequate reserve stocks for the permanent force. Consideration will have to be given by the staff as. to what is a proper and appropriate ' division under these two heads, and the balance I take it would be declared surplus and be disposed of. I am afraid that I cannot give the break-down in exactly the way my hon. friend asked for it. Cancellation charges as such are borne by the Department of Munitions and Supply.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
Ammunition and bombs, $70,525,161.

The minister is budgeting for $70,525,161. Expenditures to - September 30, 1945, were $17,123,030, which leaves a balance of $53,402,131. Since the active campaign has ended, it does seem to me that the figures are out of line, and I would imagine that there could be some paring down of this $53,000,000 odd from September 30 on.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The committee might like to have a brief break-down. As in most of these items from now on this is largely a carry-over to clean up existing commitments. Of the total estimated provision of $70,525,161. $47,058,880 represents commitments incurred prior to the beginning of this fiscal year, and $23,466,281 represents commitments incurred since April 1 last. This item is literally a clean-up item.
There is nothing in the item regarding experimental work by the minister's department?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I should not think so. There may be some small amount for -orders of new

Demobilization-Army
ammunition to round out types that we have run short of, but the item is for the straight purchase of ammunition and .bombs.
I meant new equipment that it might be desired to test and check and that might be coming in to the minister's department.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There may be some small amount in the item for that purpose, but the manufacture of ammunition and bombs has been kept up to date, and experimental work has been carried on with large scale manufacture of the ammunition itself.

The United States army the other day got what they call Little Jim, a gun with a 22-foot barrel, and they will have no opportunity of using it. I was wondering if the Canadian army was going to carry on experiments of that sort.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: There is included in the item SI 15,000 for Canadian armament research and development. That is probably what my hon. friend has in mind?
Yes.

Armament, including rifles, machine guns, mortars and guns of all descriptions, $84,006,979.
I presume the same answer would [DOT]apply here. It looks as though there had bpen previous commitments to a substantial amount. Will the minister explain?

speechtext: The carry-over here is even larger. Of the total of $84,006,979, the carryover is $57,000,000 odd, and there are new commitments subsequent to the first of April of 826,497,000.

In view of recent reports
in the press regarding the attitude of the United States with reference to having uniformity amongst the American republics in the matter of the production of arms, et cetera for the future, and in view of the fact that a senior officer of the war office in London, who is charged with responsibility for the policy in connection with arms in the British army, paid a visit to Ottawa last week, could the minister tell us the results of any conferences between this British officer and the minister or officials of his department, and indicate the policy which the Canadian army intends to follow with reference to the development of arms, either in respect of British or of United States patents? .

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am afraid I am not in a position at the moment to make any statement as to the policy. We are maintaining the closest contact with both the British and the
Americans. All members of the committee will agree, I think, that it is desirable that equipment of this kind should be standardized as much as possible. The method of achieving that desired end is one which has to be worked out. I am not in a position to make any statement as to . the results which will be achieved, except to express the fervent hope, which I know is shared by a good many others, that a satisfactory solution will be found.
Does the minister's department intend to give the various units throughout the country more equipment of different kinds of guns-I mean mortars, and so on?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
My hon. friend is referring
to reserve army units, I suppose?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes. As I said in my preliminary statement, it is our intention to see that the reserve army units have the latest and most up-to-date equipment in ample quantities. We have the quantities to give them now. Perhaps ten or fifteen years from now new weapons will be brought down, but the army to-day is well supplied with the latest and most up-to-date equipment, and that will be made available to the units of the reserve army.
Does the minister's department intend, as was done after the last war, to give guns away as ornaments for city parks and the like?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That has not been considered. If I can express a personal opinion, I am a bit against it. I never thought they added much to the aesthetic appearance of our parks.

The amount for rifles
and machine guns, so late in the war, seems rather large. Were these guns and rifles which are mentioned as being manufactured intended for the Canadian army or for some allied army?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The items here are only for our own forces. As my hon. friend knows, we manufactured fairly substantial quantities of guns and small arms for other nations under mutual aid. But that is not included in these estimates.

Is. it the intention of the
government to use the excellent camp and hospital which have been established at Prince George for training purposes in the future? Has any consideration been given to that, or does the minister intend to give any?

Demobilization-Army

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I cannot say I have given
any specific consideration to that question.' I will take note of ray hon. friend's remarks and see that the facilities at Fort George are kept in mind.

What disposal is being
made of the large number of guns, machine guns, and so forth, which were in the hands of the Canadian army overseas at the end of the war? Is it proposed to bring them back to Canada, or are they to be scrapped over there? The same question really applies to the next item; what is being done with the armoured fighting vehicles, tanks and armoured cars, which are of no use for civilian purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: In common with other surplus property of this kind they will be turned over to War Assets for disposal, presumably for disposal in Europe. If there are in Europe certain types of weapons or like equipment which are surplus to army requirements and which we need in Canada, they will be brought back, but any that are surplus will be declared surplus in Europe and War Assets will dispose of them there, or any place they see fit.
Is any of that equipment being destroyed over there?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.

Because sometimes it
might be brought back here and declared useless and put into scrap.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: None of it is being scrapped, so far as I know.

Does the minister intend to dispose of rifles? It seems to me that at the end of the last war we had a considerable number of rifles, yet when this war commenced there seemed to be a tremendous scarcity. Is it the intention of the government to retain rifles in some place and keep them in condition?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon."friend may have forgotten that after the fall of France a large numer of rifles, some 75,000, in Canada were sent over to England, and that pretty well depleted our stocks of rifles. These rifles have not been sent back.

It is a common practice in the home to remove to the attic things not required at the time, and this practice goes on year by year until, perhaps, moving day comes, and a great deal of household furniture and equipment is found to be obsolete. I am told that this sort of thing may have been going on in the armouries across the country, and that there will be found there much 
material and equipment which could far better be scrapped and disposed of. I bring this to the attention [DOT] of the minister to inquire whether this may not be a favourable time for a housecleaning in the armouries.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Yes. The point is very well taken. I understand that a review or survey is now being made and steps are being taken to get rid of obsolete equipment, turn it over to War Assets Corporation, and see if they can dispose of it.

Following my previous question, I would ask if any restrictions are placed on the sale of guns and so forth in Europe. Has the government laid down any policy as to whom these guns may be sold to? There is a distinct possibility that they might be sold, let us* say, to the Spaniards.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not so far as I am aware. It does not come under my department, -which is not a disposal department, but I understand that such negotiations as have been carried on have been with our allies-the Dutch, or French, or others who may have need of some of this equipment which we can supply.

Has any fuel been turned over by the army to War Assets?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not very much, I am advised. There has been some coal, but in the language of the deputy minister it has been turned over in outlandish places.

The minister may recall that when we were dealing with the naval estimates the member for Regina City asked a question similar to the one he asked to-day and a request was made to have the information available on the army estimates. It would give a better picture of the amount of money we are actually authorizing to be expended. We should know approximately how much will be received back for items that have been declared surplus. I would support the request of the hon. member for Regina City if that information can be made available at all. In that connection, can the minister give any information as to what boards or groups overseas are passing on this equipment and declaring what is surplus? What policy guides them? How do they make the decision, and on what basis do they determine whether to dispose of material or bring it back to Canada for disposal^

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That decision would be
made by the chief of staff overseas, the army commander, with the approval of C.M.H.Q. in London, and they would authorize it on the recommendation of the army commander. I do not know the routine, but I suppose the army commander would get a recommendation from the Q.M.G. branch, which in turn would have a recommendation from someone else, and it would move up the line until authorized at the top. To put it broadly, however, it is authorized by headquarters overseas.

Has serious consideration
been given the question whether it is worth while bringing the material back to Canada to make it available here rather than disposing of it there? I realize that it would cost a great deal, but has that been done?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I misunderstood my hon. friend. That decision would be made here. A report would be made here as to what was being declared surplus, and headquarters in Canada, as a matter of policy, would decide whether that particular type of material should be brought back to Canada or disposed of there. The final declaration to War Assets Corporation would be made in Ottawa -the declaration as to whether the material was surplus, no longer needed in the army. If the army no longer needed it in Canada *'7096-112
or in Europe, War Assets Corporation would decide whether it should be brought back or
disposed of there.

The question has been raised by the member for Regina City and the member for Kamloops as to the amount of material turned over to War Assets Corporation and they have indicated that it would help us to know how much money would be involved. I have been under the impression that whatever is turned over to War Assets Corporation has nothing to do with these estimates. If there is a credit it is a national credit rather than a departmental credit.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is correct.

I would ask the minister whether any games equipment has been turned over, such as footballs, baseball bats and so on, which have been used by soldiers and army personnel during the war, or whether such equipment is likely to be turned over in the immediate future. There is in my own home university in Saskatoon an urgent need at the present moment for such equipment, and the reason for the question is that many of the men who require it are men who used it in the armed forces. I should guess that there are about 800 military personnel attending the university of Saskatoon. The director of athletics there has applied to the department for the release of some of the equipment which cannot be obtained through ordinary channels of business, and they are particularly anxious that some should be released in the immediate future. Is there any prospect of that?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am not in a position to answer the question. Games equipment is provided by the auxiliary services, which, as my hon. friend knows, are under the jurisdiction of the Department of National War Services. The army as such does not provide games equipment. When that department is under consideration the minister will no doubt give my hon. friend the information.

I do not know under what item the question of canteen funds arises, but I would ask the minister for a statement with regard to the administration of that fund. I understand that the committee met in 1941. I was a member of it, and so far as I am aware no report has been received since that year. That fund has now reached a very considerable sum, and I understand that an advisory board has been appointed to administer it.. I would also ask the minister to give us some information with regard to N.A.A.F.I. If he cannot give it to-day perhaps he will put it on the record later on.

Demobilization-Army

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am afraid I shall have to ask my hon. friend to let the question stand, and I will try to make a statement later. The direct administration of canteen funds is not primarily an army matter, and any profits are turned over to the receiver general. There is not in the army a benevolent fund as there is in some other services. The administration of N.A.A.F.I. is something with which the Canadian army in Canada has nothing to do. I believe that in Great Britain N.A.A.F.I. services some of the camps in which our troops are stationed-perhaps all of them-and also on the continent of Europe. I did not quite catch what my hon. friend asked-with regard to N.AA.F.I.
Is it not supervised from Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No. There is no supervision by Canada of N.A.A.F.I., and other canteen services, auxiliary services, the Canadian Legion canteen and so on are under the jurisdiction of the Department of National War Services. As regards the ordinary regimental canteens, to which I suppose the hon. member for Camrose refers, the army has of course some responsibility. The regimental funds board looks after that. I will consider what my hon. friend has said and see if I can make a more extended statement.

In connection with the declaring of vehicles, tanks and so on to be surplus, and turning them over to War Assets for disposal, I would ask on what scale equipment of this kind is being retained for the use of the reserve army. The war establishment. of an anti-tank regiment is some 250 vehicles of all sorts. What proportion of these is being retained for reserve army regiments of that type?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We have not reached that point yet. We have large stocks of these vehicles available, but I do not know whether the staff has definitely determined yet how many will be kept for the reserve army. I can make this general statement, however, that ample reserves will be provided. I am not in a position to give a specific answer to my hon. friend now.

I know there are not in Canada sufficient vehicles to equip completely the six divisions which have been spoken of for the reserve army, yet there seems to be quite a bit of disposal going on. I was wondering whether any reasonable amount of equipment was going to be retained for the use of the reserve army so that it might be [Mr. Marshall.1
much better trained than the reserve army was before the war, at which time we sadly lacked equipment of all sorts.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Sufficient will be retained for full training purposes, and probably some may be brought back from the other side.

When we were discussing the naval estimates the minister gave the assurance that training in combined operations would be continued, but when I asked a question in regard to repairs to landing craft he informed me that this was dealt with under the army estimates. Would he now be able to say what proportion of this money is being spent for the repair or replacement of damaged landing craft?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I am told we have not that information, but I will see if it can be dug out of the detail at headquarters.
Mr. PEARIvES: I hope that can be done, because these landing craft are not in the same condition as they were when they started, and it is important that we carry on this training. We have the minister's assurance that it will be carried on, and I should like to be satisfied as to the cost of these repairs.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am sure the landing craft will be kept in repair, but I do not know whether it is possible to give my hon. friend the exact amount included in these estimates for the repair of landing craft. That may be included in a general estimate for repairs; I imagine it is.

I see that tractors are mentioned under this item, I should like to know from the minister whether it would include also any considerable quantity of road building equipment, and how much of such equipment has been liquidated already to the War Assets Corporation. I understand there is quite a demand on the part of various governmental bodies for surplus tractors, bulldozers and other road building equipment, and I should like some picture of the state of that item.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am afraid I can give only a very general statement. This equipment was in pretty short supply here in Canada, but I am informed that we are bringing back from the other side quite a bit of engineering equipment, which I think would include bulldozers and things of the kind.
You have no figures?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
No, I have no figures here. As I think the committee will realize, it is a little too early to give accurate figures on

Demobilization-Army
just what, will be surplus and what can be disposed of. We are still pretty much engaged in cleaning up after the end of the war and seeing where we stand-taking inventory, as it were. I think probably when we come to consider the estimates early next year we should be in a position to give definite, clear cut information as to just what is available for the civilian economy and what has to be kept in the service.

We often hear reports of the scrapping of a considerable amount of this equipment. I am inclined to agree that in many cases these reports are exaggerated, but I hope the minister will give an assurance that equipment which is usable, particularly by governmental bodies, will not be scrapped too readily.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Oh, yes. my hon. friend may rest assured that nothing will be scrapped that has usable value. He is quite right when he says there is no foundation at all in fact for these statements that valuable assets are being scrapped and thrown away.

During the war there *was need for quick delivery, messenger service and the transportation of personnel from place to place in Ottawa, and I presume at military district headquarters elsewhere. We have been accustomed to seeing on' Elgin street a procession of military vehicles, army and air force especially, far outnumbering civilian transport. It would 9eem to me there might be an opportunity, not only in regard to the army, navy and' air force but in regard to all branches of government in Ottawa, to work out some coordinated system of delivery from one department to another as a means of effecting a saving in peace-time. .1 am wondering if under this item the vote showing a reduction of perhaps fifty per cent in the amount estimated for the year, does not give some encouragement in the direction of economy. The point I should like to leave with the minister is the possibility of some coordination in dispatching and delivering about the city, where there would seem to be an opportunity of saving money.

From time to time we receive inquiries as to where these surplus vehicles are being sold and in what quantities. Can the minister tell us in what part of the country these surpluses are being declared, and the numbers that are being sold in each section?
47696-112}

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have no information as to the particular areas in which they have been declared surplus, but these surplus declarations are made right across Canada. As a vehicle became surplus in M.D. 6 it would be so declared and disposed of presumably in Halifax. The same would apply in M.D. 2, M.D. 4, M.D. 5 or any other district. They are declared surplus in the district in which they are located, and under normal circumstances are disposed1 of in that district. That has been the procedure so far.

I notice tanks mentioned in this item, together with repair parts, and so on. I should like to draw the minister's attention to a condition connected with the tank range in St. Vincent township in the county of Grey. An agreement was entered into by the army and the municipality with respect to repairs to the road, but I understand from the reeve of the municipality that the agreement has not been honoured so far as the army is concerned. Some inquiries have been made, and I am anxious to know whether the repairs referred to in this item would be repair parts only or whether anything would be included to implement the agreement concerning road repairs in St. Vincent township.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We have passed that item already. It would come under item No. 4, maintenance of property.
As long as the money is there it will be all right.

I should like to ask a question with regard to typewriters. The minister said a few moments ago there were no exceptions in regard to turning over all assets to the War Assets Corporation. On a number of occasions I have heard that typewriters were to be turned back to the companies who made them, that they were not to be put on the market. I should like the minister to say whether or not that is correct.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: If that were the case it would be simply on instructions of War Assets Corporation. We would have declared them surplus and held them subject to direction, and we would take their instructions as to where we delivered them. There should be no direct disposal by the army, of typewriters or anything else.

I understand the army does not dispose of them, because they are turned over to War Assets Corporation, Does War Assets Corporation sell them to the public,
Demobilization-Army

or are they turned back to the companies from which they were purchased in the first instance?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I do not know. I would have to give the same answer I have given before, that when the unfortunate minister who will answer the questions on behalf of War Assets Corporation is before the committee he will be able to tell my hon. friend.
Wihat information has the minister with respect to the declaring of surplus materials in Great Britain?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Probably the hon. member was not in his seat when^I discussed that in detail only a short time ago. The procedure there is substantially the same as it is here. Headquarters in London will decide which properties should be declared surplus. That information is forwarded to N.D.H.Q. here.
Has the minister information as to the quantities?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not the quantities, no.
The minister cannot give the committee the quantities of such materials declared surplus?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No. I probably could get the information, but it is not before me now. Material is being declared surplus practically all the time.

With respect to bulldozers and road equipment, may I point out that in my province, there is a great shortage of road equipment of various types, especially tractors and bulldozers. As the committee is aware, during the war we were allowed only a small quota from the United States, where we got most of that equipment. The result was that to a large extent bridges were neglected, and to-day many municipalities are faced with the necessity of repairing bridges for the winter months. In some plac.es efforts are being made to secure some of these bulldozers and tractors from the army, the air force, or any other branch of the service. As the minister has said, they have not yet been declared surplus. I understand that at the present time the authorities are in process of taking stock. Is there any possibility of cutting a few corners or getting rid of red tape with a view to speeding up the turning over of this type of equipment to War Assets Corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I shall see if we can speed it up as much as possible.
*'Mr. Brooks.]

The information I obtained from the branch of War Assets Corporation in Winnipeg was that all typewriters would be sold back to the original companies I spent a couple- of hours discussing this matter with the authorities, and that was the information they gave me.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
May I remind hon.
members that the item before the committee does not deal with War Assets Corporation. Those items will be discussed later. We would expedite matters if hon. members would withhold their questions in that connection until the appropriate estimates are before us.

These questions have
developed from the minister's statement that all assets were being disposed of to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No.
That was the general statement the minister made.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: No, not "to the public". I do not know where they are being disposed of. I said that when we no longer required them in the army we declared them surplus. They are handled by the crown assets allocation committee. Then they go to War Assets Corporation for disposal.

We understand that, and we will have to get our answers from the minister in charge of War Assets Corporation. I understand that soldiers are given preference in the purchase of war assets being turned back in the United States. Have any representations been made by his or other service departments to War Assets Corporation to give returned men preference in the purchase of these assets? I understand that in the United States such assets are being disposed to returned soldiers at low prices.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Department of Veterans Affairs has made strong representations to the War Assets Corporation along the lines suggested by the hon. member.
Has there been any action?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: The action seems to be quite favourable, I can tell my hon. friend.
Keep pressing.
Do I understand you to say, Mr. Chairman, that at a later time we will have an opportunity to discuss the operations of War Assets Corporation?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
War Assets Corporation comes under the Department of Reconstruction. When that department is before the committee, members will have an opportunity to ask their questions.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
It is understood that
there are no sales at all from defence departments.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That is my understanding of it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Of surplus goods.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Correct.

At what point is a training centre turned over to AVar Assets Corporation? Let us suppose that the occupants of the centre are moved out, and that only'a skeleton staff remains. Under such circumstances, when is it turned over? Is it under the supervision of the department, or that of War Assets Corporation?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: When a training establishment is no longer required we declare it surplus, just as we do any other type of equipment, and War Assets Corporation takes it over. There may be a period of a week or two, or perhaps a month, when War Assets Corporation might not have the staff to look after it; I am not sure as to that. Under such circumstances we may do a caretaking job for a month or so. But once the army is through with it, and it is declared surplus, the primary responsibility is with War Assets Corporation for care and disposal.

I would draw the min- ' ister's attention to the opposite item in the naval estimates, and would point out that he left several questions unanswered. I am not demanding that the answers be given before his items are passed, but I am simply reminding him that if he could give the answers as soon as possible it would be helpful.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I think I have almost all that naval information ready, but I thought I might wait until we had finished these estimates, at which time I could take a few minutes and give all the information at one time. *
I am not even asking the minister to do that. I am simply reminding him.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I have not forgotten.

What disposition has been
made of the world grain show building in Regina? Has it been turned back to the city by the department? If not, when can we expect to get it back? Has the General Motors building been taken over for the maintenance of Department of National Defence vehicles?

speechtext: The first property to which reference is made is being used as a demobilization centre in Regina, and will be required for that purpose for some time. Disposition of the second building referred to is under active" consideration.

Item agreed to.

There was a question about the reserve army I wished to ask the minister. As he knows, these men have done a good job during the war in certain parts of Canada. Many of them are older men, ranging in age from forty-five to sixty years. Would it be possible, nowT that the war is finished and their job is over, for those men to get their discharges from the army? Will any recognition be given the reserve army for their services during the war? As the minister knows, certain sections of the eastern coast were set aside for defence by these men. They were called out at odd times of the day and night, and they rendered very good service. I should like to know also the strength of the reserve army at the present time.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
On the first point, we are
now giving consideration to what should be done about allowing the members of the reserve army, who as my hon. friend has said have rendered such outstanding service during the war, to leave the organization. As my hon. friend says, they are mostly older men and they have done a great job. Perhaps I should not make the statement on the floor of the house, but I do not think very much would be done if they did not show up at parade three times a week. What we really hope for is that they will hang on a bit longer to allow the lads to get back from overseas. Many of these men will have had combat experience; they will be much younger men, and they may want to join the reserve army. The whole question whether these men should be permitted to relinquish their work is now under careful consideration.
If I may express a personal opinion I think that some recognition should be made of their services. As to what form that will take, again we have not been able to decide whether
Demobilization-Army

it should be a button or whether some special consideration might be given to their accelerated service qualifying them for the long service medal for service in the reserve army during the war when their duties were much greater than they would have been in peace time. The whole picture is being looked at, and I may say most sympathetically. I hope to be able to make some announcement at an early day.
The latest report I have as to the strength of the reserve army is as of August 31, 1945. This gives the strength as 4,470 officers and 59.938 other ranks.
The hon. member for Nanaimo asked what provision was being made for the maintenance of landing craft. I have been advised that provision for maintenance has been made and that the landing craft are currently being kept on a care and maintenance basis.
Could the minister break up this item into subsections so that we shall have some idea as to what is covered here?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
The first large item is
$2,915,258 of a carryover from the preceding fiscal year. The total item of $13,394,771 falls under three headings. First, there is printing and stationery, $4,063,527. Then there is special training equipment, $614,000 and sundries, $8,717,244. I shall give a little detail as to the sundries. Special educational films, production of films and news reels, $124,500. Rehabilitation training programme overseas, $50,000. I am just giving some of the larger items. The list is a long one, but it is available to any hon. member who wants to see it. Research and information, publication of army bulletin Khaki, C.W.A.C. news letter, $160,000. Sports programme, $125,000. Broadcast service to personnel of army forces in United Kingdom and theatres of operation, $28,000. Concert parties and army shows, $177,100. Inventions board, $50,000. Pacific coast mountain rangers, administration expenses, $120,000. That is part of the carry-over. Wireless construction, antennae networks and ground systems, $140,000. That is under communications service; there is an item of $2,216,900 for that.
The minister mentioned overseas speakers. Should not that come under the wartime information board? Should not the item for educational films come under the national film board?

speechtext: Those are special expenditures which the army makes for its own account.
Can the minister give us any information about the revenue derived from the army shows?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I am advised that we do not get much revenue. The army shows are generally shown to the troops. I shall get that information and give it to my hon. friend later.

I understand the
minister cannot give us the figures with regard [DOT] to the materials that have been declared surplus, either by the army in Canada or in Great Britain.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: Not at the moment.
Can they be provided for this committee?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I would doubt it. The deputy minister tells me that it is done periodically. It is available the same as any information of that kind, but just how soon I would not care to say.

Billions of dollars have been spent on the army, and the materials are an asset of the Canadian people. The Canadian people have paid for them, and they would like to know what disposition has been made of them.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: My hon. friend will recall that there is a notice of motion on the order paper to set up a committee, which I imagine will make an exhaustive inquiry into the operations of the War Assets Corporation, and that is the place where the information will be made available.
Quite correct. But War Assets will have nothing to do with any of these things until after the minister's department has declared them surplus.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
That is correct.

speechtext:

Mr. LaCROIX (Translation): Mr. Chairman, for some time past, hon. members who are surely entitled to express their own views, have been unanimous in their request for the establishment, in peace-time Canada, of a considerable fighting force, or, if you prefer, of a first-rate army-

speechtext:

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I asked the minister a question the other day, on Tuesday, I think, with respect to the N.R.M.A. He answered it in part on Wednesday, at which time he gave the enrolment in that organization by years. Yesterday he gave the estimated cost by years of that organization. In giving this further answer he stated:
Here is the estimated figure for each fiscal year based on per capita cost for personnel costs only:
Then he gave the costs for each of half a dozen years, totalling some $246,000,000. In my question the other day I asked if the answer would include overhead. I ask the minister now' if he will explain how he arrived at this cost.

speechtext:
Yes, I have given that explanation. "Personnel costs" includes the following items: Pay and allowances; travel and transportation; operating expenses of
properties; clothing and necessaries; personal equipment; barrack stores; rations; medical stores; dental stores; printing and stationery. The per capita estimate includes these items of cost. I am advised that that is as close to it as we can get. '

speechtext: The reason I ask the question is this. In making a rough calculation, taking first of all the numbers in the organization and then the figures of cost for each year, it looks to me to be an exceedingly small figure, varying in different years from $200 per individual-those individuals probably were not in for the whole year-up to $500 for the whole year. It looks a pretty small estimate of the cost.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext:
I did not make the estimate myself. I asked the officials of the department to make as accurate an estimate as they could of the cost. It is obvious, of course, that such can only be an estimate. There was not an N.R.M.A. organization as such. Each of these men was with other soldiers in establishments for the Canadian Army as a whole. I think that that figure probably reflects pretty accurately the cost of these men. Of course there is the further point, as I mentioned in my opening statement, that of the 158,000 odd who came into the N.R.M.A. with that status, something like 57,000 to
58,000	volunteered for general service in the army and others volunteered for one of the other two services.

speechtext: Could the minister give the total strength of the force in say the year 1944? I know it would vary a little bit from time to time, but the enrolment by years does not give the strength in any particular year.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: I can give the number of men having N.R.M.A. status in the Canadian Army at any given date. I have not the figures here, but could get them very quickly. For the sake of illustration, I could take December 31, 1944 or some date close to that; w'ould that satisfy my hon. friend?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Yes. Is there any way of arriving at the average strength in a given year? Is there any such figure?

On the outbreak of war a number of enemy aliens and Canadian citizens were detained under the defence of Canada regulations and it was agreed between the Canadian and the British governments that Canada should receive a number of enemy prisoners of war and refugees for internment in this country. Mr. WILFRID LaCROIX (Translation): Mr. Chairman, for some time certain hon. members of this house, who most assuredly are entitled to their own opinions, have been urging the setting up in this country during peace time of large armed forces or, if you prefer, of a first-rate army with conscription as the form of enlistment, as was advocated by the honourable member for St. Boniface (Mr. Viau) and by many other honourable members of this house.
I have too much respect for the honourable members to insinuate that such propaganda is inspired by the legitimate desire on the part of brass hats to keep their high-salaried positions, because a good many among them would find it difficult to obtain comparable employment in civil life. Let me tell you
tUr. Abbott.]
that the inevitable result of the organization in this country of a big army would be the continuance of the exorbitant taxes which people in the lower salary brackets now have to pay, as well as the maintaining of the far too numerous controls which dominate and paralyse private enterprise to such a degree that it is extremely difficult for any ambitious young man to start a new industry or business, because he is denied the quota of goods he would need for that purpose. In short, it Would mean the dictatorship of the military caste to the financial prejudice of every one among us.
In view of our geographical position and our small population of 12,000,000 we cannot launch out into such an- adventure. I feel that, on the contrary, all the financial resources of a young country like purs should be devoted to its development with a view' to eliminating unemployment which unfortunately, is already being experienced. As a matter of fact, how can a manufacturer or a business man face the problems of the future if the burden of his obligations toward the government is maintained at its present rate?
Let us rather endeavour to create in this country a first rate agricultural and industrial wealth. Is not a country which has reached such a position through the development of its huge natural resources a decisive factor - in a war, as was evidenced by the United States in the last conflict, even though that country did not have conscription during peace time.
The more powerful our military organization is, the more apt it will be to become a factor which a prospective enemy would endeavour, to the limit of its powers, to destroy as constituting an obstacle to its ends and, therefore, a cause of future armed conflict between our country and this theoretical enemy. I claim that military training in peace time, if exaggerated, might well be an endeavour to apply in our country the worst pre-war European methods, which, as you are aware, have led and would still inevitably lead to war.
On this subject here is what the archbishop of Boston had to say. Although his military knowledge and experience may, with reason, be doubted, we must nevertheless admit that he gives us an example of common sense and logic which, in my estimation, should be the guiding principles of our future policy. I quote:
Ever since Napoleon resorted to conscription in peace time and Prussia followed his bad example, such a system has inevitably resulted in dictatorship, militarism and competition in

armaments. This system has been a curse' to Europe and it has paralysed its culture. God fo -bid that we apply here the worst theories of the old world. Compulsory military training, discredited to such an extent in Europe, must not encumber our post-war programme. Let all American statesmen take the lessons of history. All the nations who lost the second world war had conscription in peace time. They have been bled white, both morally and physically. Such is the infallible result of conscription in peace time.
I have no objection to a well disciplined army, as long as it remains in proportion with our population and financial resources; what I object to is the arming of the whole nation.
Here is, on this subject, an excerpt from an outstanding newspaper of our province, VAction catholique:
Had the European nations maintained permanent armies instead of organized armed peoples, the last two wars would not have unleashed such a storm of destruction. If Canada is really a peace-loving nation wishing to bury the hatchet for good, why does it not take the lead and set an example in disarmament? That argument, however, is not the only one used by those who favour compulsory military service, but this proposal is put forward only by a few enlightened individuals who are real busy-bodies.
The other protagonists are more dangerous for they invoke subtle arguments. They use the sentimental appeal and put forward two reasons: the need of physical training and the dream of bringing about in Canada unity of thought with all that it implies, as if two different cultures could no longer develop side by side in our country.
The need of physical training is obvious. Education, however, is a provincial responsibility. There can be no bargaining or backing down on this issue. Moreover, it is far from proved that military service in itself is the best means of building up sound men. It is better to insist on the necessity of entrusting physical education to the schools, which means to. the parents themselves, since this is part of their duty. It is better to develop young people's taste for physical exercise, life in the open and the building up of their muscles through sports while making them conscious of their personality. Military training often becomes nothing more than plain unadulterated regimentation. -
Next comes the need for developing better citizens. In this sphere, f>ropaganda is right in its element. It tends to mould all Canadians to the same pattern, to fashion minds that will find legislative union more and more acceptable.
Further:
For reasons as varied as the need of adventure and the improvement of business relations, with the added attraction of the Anglo-Saxon standard of living, there are far too many who, every year, go over to the other camp. On the other hand, the relish derived from conquest and the tendency to assimilate remain deep-rooted among some of our Anglo-Saxon fellow-citizens. According to their character, they still stalk their prey, using bold or subtle methods.
All things considered, the arguments put forward in favour of compulsory military service are almost baseless. They are designed only for people who, because of the war, have lost all control over their feelings.
We are on slippery ground and must climb a very steep hill. Our reaction must be all the stronger to counterbalance a more insidious and constant propaganda. It is the will that founts, and we must will it decidedly.
We may rightly wonder if the enforcement . of peace-time conscription for military service in Canada will not lead to moral disintegration which will prevent future generations from playing a useful part in solving the problems of their day, especially when opinions such as those voiced by Major-General Chisholm who is a senior administrative officer and a high-ranking member of the army, are expressed.
I wish to refer to a recent pronouncement, in Ottawa, of the deputy minister of National Health and Welfare. To my mind, such an utterance would warrant his immediate release by his superior, the Minister of Health (Mr. Cla'xton). I quote:
The idea of good and evil is a myth created by politicians, priests and others interested in keeping us under their domination.
This is not the first blunder of the major-general, for it is he, who, during the war, claimed that sexual laxity was a necessity for soldiers. Therefore, this deputy minister is amoral by his own admission and should be shown the door without delay.
I am certainly not convinced that the inception of a two or three-year compulsory military training programme wou!4. give us a bette'r class of citizens. This policy of a first-class conscripted army has always been the first plank of the Tory platform, for the members of that party know that it would be a factor of closer intimacy with the empire; and is not imperialism the keystone of their doctrine?
It is also a tenet of the Social Credit party, whose leader, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low) stated, in this house, on September 28 last, as reported in Hansard:
While we are making Canada strong, we must at the same time be prepared to contribute of our strength to ensure the preservation of Britain. Britain is in danger. Britain is in a serious condition. If Great Britain is destroyed the British commonwealth of nations cannot endure; therefore we must be prepared to contribute of our strength to ensure that Britain will remain strong and virile, and that the British commonwealth of nations will be maintained.
I do not believe the French Canadians will ever get fair play in the Canadian army, for, of all the parties represented in this house,
