the Liberal party has the most sympathy for them, and in spite of their efforts and good intentions,'they have failed, during the war, to prevent discrimination being shown against them. How could they get better results in peace time when all our imperialistic brass hats will be enshrined in high army posts to form a class accountable to no one. Of course-, certain improvements could be implemented, but, as a whole, the imperialistic views will prevail. These views require that the French Canadians have as little influence as possible in the army, because, as a class, they are the most devoted to the Canadian fatherland.
Allow me, however, to congratulate the Minister of Defence for his worthy efforts at the present time, in favour of Canadians of French descent. I would also like to acknowledge the evident good will of the Minister for Air (Mr. Gibson) who stated, in a letter he sent me on November 1:
In our post-war plans and in recognition of the splendid record established by the all French-Canadian squadron No. 425 overseas, it has been more or less definitely decided to establish a permanent R.C.A.F. station at Ancienne Lorette.
In order that you may be familiar with the magnitude of such a step, may I outline in brief just what a station such as this incorporates:
(1)	A permanent V.L.R. (very long range) squadron (heavy bomber-Lancaster) will be in operation.
(2)	In addition, an auxiliary squadron detachment will be in operation.
(3)	In addition, a V.H.F. (very high frequency) Homersite will be operated.
(4)	To permit the above to function, a station headquarters will be established.
(5)	All in all, the station strength will approximate twelve hundred personnel.
(6)	Further to the above operations, the Department of Transport will be in position and, 1 understand, plan to operate a commercial flying base utilizing large four engine planes, thus establishing a No. 1 airport.
(7)	In order to adapt the existing station to meet operational requirements for the above, the runways will be extended giving temporary employment to several hundred men.
(8)	Further, changes, extensions and alterations to existing buildings and construction of new buildings will be required to provide the requisite accommodation.
(9)	As the station strength will constitute in great part of married personnel, the population of the station will be proportionately increased.
Therefore, you will gather that in order to honour the reputation of No. 425 squadron, we have very ambitious plans for Ancienne Lorette. the effects of which should be very material throughout the Quebec area.
I have striven for ten years, since I have entered this house, to have the need of a national flag and a national anthem recognized.

May I sincerely congratulate the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) for the steps which he has taken to ensure the achievement of this goal. I believe that this is the result of the vision and the tenacious efforts of his close associate, the Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent). I hope that any sign of colonialism will disappear from that flag.
But if French Canadians are to secure the share and influence to which they are entitled in the army, the present Minister of National Defence-who, I know, is sympathetic to the French Canadians-will have to roll up his sleeves and assert his authority and make a thorough clean-up of the headquarters staff. I sincerely hope that he will succeed but I have my doubts in this regard.
At any event, if there are possibilities of creating in our army a true Canadian spirit, it is certainly not with the Tories or with the Social Credit party that this goal will be attained; indeed we are aware of the views already expressed in this house by their respective leaders in this connection. Hence my confidence in the generous and unselfish endeavours of the Liberal party leaders along this line. To attain success, I repeat that it will be necessary to eliminate the spiritual influence from London which still subsists within that party for I am convinced, as I have always been for that matter, that the best means for our country to attain full maturity is the complete severance of our ties with Great Britain.
We should reply "no" to the suggestion contained in the book by George Grant, entitled "Canada must choose-the empire yes or no," which the members have received recently. We should, as I say, answer "no"; we should direct our policies towards the complete independence of our country and cooperate with the United States in the solution of our future problems in keeping, of course, with our financial resources and our ability. Indeed, I am convinced that if, to-morrow-, England should have some difficulties in some corner of her far-flung empire, to put down an uprising for independence in India, for .instance, our country, inspired as always by Downing street, will hasten to send at our expense an expeditionary force as she did at the time of the Transvaal conflict.
Some people condemn the stand taken by Ireland and the Irish in the w-ar that has recently ended, but anyone who takes the trouble to study the political history of that country will readily understand that attitude.

Demobilization-Army
Every member of this house is aware of my aversion for war and militarism, but my stand would be quite different were I convinced that Canada alone was concerned.
Besides, if our country enjoyed full independence, could we not play on this north American continent the part that was played by Switzerland in all European wars?
The honourable member for Bonaventure (Mr. Arsenault) explained the other day why defaulters or deserters are so numerous in the province of Quebec. All the reasons he adduced are true and I support him. That is why, in concluding, I shall take the liberty to ask the government to consider those reasons and grant at once to deserters a general and unrestricted amnesty. Let the government take into consideration the fact that there is at this time a. tremendous labour shortage in the forests and on our farms and let them hasten to grant deserters their release, which would help these two basic industries of the Canadian economy to carry out the heavy tasks which the UNRRA expects them to fulfil, while it would also enable deserters to participate in the relief of distress in Europe.
(Text.)

Mr. Chairman, in opening my remarks a few moments ago I pointed out that we had moved into a new era. I referred also to the tremendous development that had taken place in weapons. I suggest to the committee that the development of [DOT] those weapons has made the defence of Canada a far more difficult and pressing problem than it has been during the lifetime of anyone in this chamber. We have another problem presented by the fact that we shall be under commitment to the united nations organization. A development that occurred in the last few days is even more serious. I refer to the statement made this week by President Truman that the United States, the United Kingdom and Canada are in effect the trustees of atomic force. All of these developments mean that we must give the most careful consideration to our defence forces.
The plan submitted by the government during the discussion of these estimates is that we shall have an active army and a reserve army. The active army is to be composed of a small trained field force with, I presume, three or four infantry battalions and two armoured regiments with certain artillery. In any event it is to be quite a small field force.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: But representative of all arms.

Representative of all arms, yes. The remainder of the 20,000 or 25,000 personnel in the active army are to be used for training and research and other activities of that kind.
On the other hand, the reserve army is intended to be the back-bone of Canada's defence forces. The minister expressed that in a few words, to be found on page 1136 of Hansard, when he said:
. . . this important force which will form the background of any future military endeavour . . .
The minister said that the reserve army would comprise six divisions, with armoured troops and other supporting troops. I am not quite clear as to the total, but I think he said, between 130.000 and 150,000.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: That was an estimate on my part and I would not want to be held to that figure.
In any event the reserve army will be much stronger than it ever was before.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Minister of National Defence for Naval Services
speechtext: We hope so.

In addition to 'those six divisions, the reserve force would be responsible for coastal defence and for anti-aircraft defence. At the present time the strength of this force is about 60,000, so that there will have to be a great increase in the number. The plans are indefinite. I do not think anyone will question that statement, but I admit that it would be difficult to have definite plans at this stage.
We must remember that after the last war the Canadian corps came back to Canada with a wonderful record of being the best equipped and most efficient fighting force in Europe; yet it was not very long before our defence force had been terribly weakened. We do not want to have the same development take place after this war. The government should be warned against sliding back to the 1939 outlopk, and there are signs that that is the trend. General George C. Marshall made a statement this week which applies to Canada just about as strongly as it applies to the United States. He is quoted as using these words:
For the moment, in a widespread emotionai crisis of the American people, ' demobilization has become in effect, disintegration not only

Demobilization-A rmy
of the armed forces but apparently of all conception of world responsibility and what it demands of us.
Then there were these further words:
We must somehow get it clear in our thinking that the fulfilment of our responsibilities is not some vague mumbo-jumbo. It requires positive active effort and' sacrifice, and above all it is a continuing process.
We in the official opposition believe that the carrying out of the plans for Canada's army of the future will be a big undertaking. We think it will be a difficult job for this government to carry out that plan and that it would be a difficult job for any government. First of all, there is the recruiting. The government will have to raise nearly 200,000 for the active army and for the reserve army. That in itself is a tremendous job; nothing approaching it has ever been done before in peace time.
Then the training will be quite difficult. There is no use in having a reserve army made up of men who have had practically nc training. I was not in this war so that I cannot speak with any authority, but I do know that because of mechanical developments the soldier had to know far more than did the soldier in the last war. If there is ever a war in the future, the soldier of that time will have to know a lot more than the soldier of to-day. I do not think we should run away with the idea that we can have a fully trained reserve army by giving them one night a week and a week at camp in the summer. The training question is a difficult one. It also involves getting the consent of the employers of the men in the forces for them to take time off to go to camp. It is not going to be easy at all. The question of equipment will become very difficult in future yeans. It is all right now because we have the equipment from the war but within a year or two that equipment will be obsolete and we shall have to keep on getting modern and up-to-date equipment.
The most difficult job of all will be to build up the support of the Canadian people behind these two armies, the active army and the reserve army. I do not believe that our people are in the frame of mind now to support those armies. It has never been done in Canada; it is something entirely new. It will require very strong leadership if these plans are to be carried out. We believe, too, that the time element is very important, that if the government lets the whole question ride over for a few months and does not point out to the people how difficult the problem will be, then it may be too late. In six months or in a year our chance may be gone. We believe that if a defence force
[*Mr. Green.]
is to be built up along the lines suggested by the minister he must tell the Canadian people of the plans at as early a date as possible; tell them the position; tell them what Canada's new and important position in world affairs calls for in the way of defence forces; tell them of the vital needs.
If that is done, and I think all parties in the house would cooperate because there is nothing political about this question-it is far too serious to be the subject of political controversy-I believe that the Canadian people will respond just as they have responded to every other appeal that has been made in that spirit. You see, Mr. Chairman, a satisfactory settlement of this question may involve the survival of Canada as a nation, so that I would ask that the government lose no time and spare no effort to see that these plans are carried through to a successful conclusion. The hon. member for Regina City (Mr. Probe) asked: What are the amounts to be voted for civil salaries and pay and allowances for H.M.C.S. Queen of Regina for 1945-46?
The answer is that no provision is made for civil salaries in these estimates. Two Grade 2 clerks were taken on at the end of September 1945, for a period of about four months in connection with demobilization operations. No provision was made in the estimates for this expenditure in this particular establishment. Sufficient funds are available, however, to meet it.
As to pay and allowances, the estimated permanent establishment at the Regina division is 1 officer and 3 ratings. The amount provided for this number of personnel for pay and allowances during the seven months period from September 1, 1945, to March 31, 1946, is S3,598. The present staff consists of 9 officers and 44 ratings of whom 8 officers and 41 ratings will be demobilized at a later date. The pay and allowances of these 8 officers and 41 ratings is provided for in the general provision for personnel who will be demobilized. Some additional personnel are, at the present time, temporarily on the strength of H.M.C.S. Queen, principally in connection with the demobilization of naval personnel.
The hon. member for York South asked for the number of admirals, vice admirals and rear admirals and captains on the strength of the navy to-day. DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to delay the committee longer than necessary but I should like to make a few remarks in regard to air force policy. In the beginning of the debate on the defence estimates the hon. member for Nanaimo as an army officer paid the air force a tribute which was undoubtedly very acceptable and generous in every way. As a member of the air force I do not propose to attempt anything of that order, for I think the public of Canada are for the most part aware of the tremendous achievements of the Royal Canadian Air Force during the war-accomplishments in mobilization, construction engineering, supplying of services, training and fighting in partnership with the allied nations. In this fighting instrument, which our country had such a great part in developing, we had without doubt the most powerful offensive weapon that has ever been evolved in the history of warfare, and as such we as members of this committee should regard it during the discussion of these estimates of the air force.
In beginning I would quote, just to prove to the committee that that is not my own assessment of my own service, General Marshall in his biennial report as chief of staff of the United States army, published in the New York Times on Wednesday, October 10, 1945:
Both Keitel and Jodi believed that the invasion could be repulsed or at worst contained, and both named the allied air arm as the decisive factor in German failure.

Demobilization-Air Services
There we have great military experts paying their tribute to our air arm.
We must now turn our minds to the contemplation of this weapon from a peace-time point of view. The first thing that comes into our' minds is naturally atomic energy and the atomic bomb. I do not propose to attempt any statement on that to-day. It has been taken care of in the press by authorities, and it is moreover on a level that places it beyond discussion by the average inember of this house. It has, however, brought, the time factor in the strategy of war into prominence, and this time factor is tlie thing that we must keep before us in considering all the estimates for the defence forces. In other words, there will not be- time in the next war to mobilize, to debate, to talk and so on. We must be ready if there is another war. The appreciation of the war by General Marshall is printed in full in this issue of the New York Times, and some of the conclusions in it affect Canada and may prove very useful to this committee as a guide in our discussion of our defence estimates. Suffice it, however, to say that our destiny, security and freedom as a nation are completely linked with those of our cousin the United States of America. Speaking of the United States, let me quote some of the things that General Marshall says:
In good conscience this nation can take little credit for its part in staving off disaster in the critical days of 1942.
And again:
It is certain that the refusal of the British and Russian peoples to accept defeat was the great factor in the salvage of our civilization.
From the first quotation is it not plain to us that there is a tremendous necessity for preparedness against a future conflict of any kind, and from the second quotation is it not apparent to us that we must have the soundest of political institutions in order that our *people may have the fortitude to refuse to accept defeat under any circumstances?
Here is a third quotation:
Dissension among the enemy nations and lack of long-range planning may well have been the decisive factors in this world struggle in its most critical moments.
He says that, after he has proved that two or three times during this war Germany, Japan and Italy were on the verge of achieving a strategic position from which it would have taken us years to dislodge them. He says that dissension in their own ranks was the factor which caused the failure of our enemies. Here we have an example of dissension. Can we not bring this home to the people of our own country? Can we not cite the political difficulties of France as the cause of her failure
to fight the war as thoroughly and as successfully as the common man in France wished it to be fought? Can we not say that it is the responsibility of all leaders in this country to put away any dissension from our nation, any dissension they might cause themselves? And wdien I speak of leaders I do not mean only the representatives of constituencies in the House of Commons; I mean religious leaders, leaders of different racial groups, labour and management. Is this not a lesson to us that if we become so divided in this country we, too, may suffer from the application of the old maxim, "divide and conquer,'' and become an easy victim to an aggressor in the future?
Here is. a further quotation:
We may elect again to depend on others, and the whim and error of potential enemies, but if we do we will be carrying the treasure and freedom of this great nation in a paper bag.
That is what General Marshall says, speaking of the United States, that- if they elect to depend on others, on the whim and error of their potential enemies, then the future of their country will be as secure as if it were in a paper bag.
As hon. members of this committee know, our national security is undoubtedly vested in our armed forces. The air estimates are before the committee now, and I should like to advance this statement by General Marshall to urge that we should study them most carefully. We should be prepared to say so if we think they are not sufficient, as well as if we think they are too great; we must be prepared to err on the one side as well as on the other in connection with these estimates.
Here is a further quotation, having to do with morale:
The appearance of an unusually effective Weapon or of a particularly attractive item of enemy equipment usually provoked animated public discussion in this country-
That refers to the United States, of course. -especially when stimulated by the criticism of the army's supposed failures to provide the best. Such incidents posed a very difficult problem for the war department. In the first place, the morale of the fighting man is a matter of primary importance. To destroy his confidence in his weapons or in the higher command-is the constant and intense desire of the enemy. Americans have active imaginations. They always want the newest weapons. They might endow' the enemies' new'est weapons with extraordinary qualities, thus giving the greatest help to him by informing the enemy which of his weapons is hurting us most.
That quotation bears directly upon the responsibility of the press as well as the responsibility of public leaders, that they control their remarks and statements during

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I wish to congratulate the hon. member upon his helpful address when dealing with the air force. He has brought out many items which I think should be discussed in committee. I agree with him entirely in his remarks to the effect that the time element is one of the most important in the air force. We realize that any post-war force must be ready and available at all times. That is the basis upon which we are working in preparing for our post-war course.
The hon. member asked two questions, the first of which- was whether the estimates contained any amount for research. In item 10 we find the amount of $1,000,000 for aircraft designing and development, and in item 14 there is the sum of $434,586 for sundry projects being investigated at the present time.
His second question dealt with standardizing our equipment with that of the United States. While we are not standardizing in the manner he indicated, at the same time we are keeping close liaison with everything that is going on in that country by way of development. Our joint staff mission in Washington is keeping abreast with all developments in that country.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I note that we are asked to pass estimates amounting to $613,625,654. I believe the Canadian people are looking to the committee to present an air force policy which will justify this expenditure, and which will make possible our ability to meet the constantly changing picture which appears on the scientific front. This is a condition which affects not only the air force, but also the army and the navy.
The people of Canada want to be assured that, after having signified- our willingness to take part with the united nations in an effort to put teeth into the force which will maintain peace throughout the world, we shall be able to make a worth while contribution, and one which will reflect credit on our country. I can readily understand that, until our commitments to the united nations organization are agreed upon, the minister may have some difficulty in properly defining this policy, and drafting a complete programme. Replying to the last speaker the minister said he had about $1,500,000 for research. It occurs to me that that amount is too small, when we realize that out of more than $613 million we are appropriating only $1,500,000 for research.
The field of scientific research is changing so rapidly that even within the last six months we have seen a change which makes obsolete equipment which that short time ago we thought was superior and essential to our defen'ce. I doubt whether Canada can maintain her position in the field of research and as an effective unit among the united nations unless she is prepared to spend a greater proportion of her money and her effort in that regard.
The operation of the British commonwealth training plan in Canada has been one of the bright spots in Canada's contribution to the war. We are pleased to note that in their drafting of air force policy, ministers who have headed that department have, decided to maintain at different points throughout Canada certain permanent air force training ports, where training may continue. The personnel which will man the defence system of Canada, and that of the united nations for the prevention of future war, is of utmost-importance. Canada's success in the field of air operations, one of her greatest successes, has arisen from the fact that out of our civilian population we were able to produce personnel who could take hold of the job of administration and of the development of scientific research, and transform it into an actual fighting, combat force which could be used effectively.
The contribution made by Canadian airmen in the last war was one of the greatest, one of which Canada is proud, and I believe we should try to maintain that record. Where did those men come from? They came from our schools, because Canadian youth is air-minded. Our public schools, and particularly our high schools are filled with young men who are attracted by the field of aviation. They study plans and types of aircraft, and they should be given an opportunity to develop those natural talents they possess.
My suggestion would be that a larger proportion of these estimates might be devoted to this purpose. No doubt the minister will outline his plan with regard to the maintenance, perhaps not of a cadet corps which would emphasize the military side of activities, but rather of a group who would study scientific advancement in aviation. Young men who show promise and who have the physical stamina should be encouraged to come forward, and should be given an opportunity to carry on studies where they could attend lectures conducted by those who understand the technique of aeronautical engineering, and are in touch with the latest scientific advancement. Those young men who ^how promise should be encouraged, even to the
Demobilization-Air Services

extent of being given scholarships, so that they might go on to university and receive their bachelor of science degree. I would not so much favour a military college, which is apt to become too much bound up with red tape and to be hemmed in with unnecessary army discipline. I would prefer that civilians of the proper type and having the required ability might be given the facilities for continuing their courses. Such aeronautical courses could be made optional in connection with the attainment of a degree of bachelor of science. Them those men in select groups might go to a permanent training camp, so that in the advanced field of flying we could provide a force of men who would be constantly trained and who would have university courses always available to them. Such men could go back into civilian life as a je serve.
Some sort of central body will have to be maintained. I rmderstand, of course, that the minister will have some difficulty in estimating exactly how many men he will require in such a force. There should be training centres where civilians could be given refresher courses and advanced training.
I do not think enough credit has been given by Canada to the men of the groundcrew, the men who manned the ships, who worked out in the hangars, the men who as the army went into France were under such terrific conditions of combat. A great deal could1 be done in our technical schools toward training groundcrew. If we had a series of flying clubs across Canada and a number of these air training schools carried on on a peace-time basis, we could then fulfil most efficiently the effort we are to be called upon to make in our contribution to the united nations. We would then be able to maintain a force, not necessarily for war but for the maintenance of peace. That should be our objective.
I cannot see how we could expect the Canadian people at this time, because of the constantly changing scene to undertake a large expenditure of money to maintain a large permanent force. The engines we had a year ago are obsolete to-day. Recently we had an opportunity of seeing a jet-propelled plane in operation. That certainly is an advance which puts much of the material upon which we spent hundreds of millions of dollars almost out of the picture.
I should like the minister to state what his plans are with regard to the preparing and training in Canada of a large civilian force with at least a fairly large number of men who are expert in the most advanced type of training. I should like to know something of his jelans so far as expanding the amount which he has said he is giving toward that

work is concerned. I should like to know if it is the policy of his department to maintain the air force separately, or whether they will work in conjunction with the army and navy. I should like to know also whether the research work will be carried on separately. These are [DOT] things in which the people of Canada are interested.	'

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
When I made my statement when the estimates were first brought down I outlined what the future policy of the air force was in as definite terms as it was possible to use at the present time. We have a planning committee working on a plan for a post-war air force. As has previously been announced, we are working on the basis of a force of ten regular squadrons: three bomiber, three fighter, three transport and one photo squadron. In addition to that, we shall have the necessary auxiliary units. It is realized that this is not a large force. First we must decide whether we are going to train a lot of men. If we trained a lot of men, we could not afford the planes that would be required. On the other hand, if we equipped the force with the latest planes in large numbers, we would not be able to keep the personnel that would be required to fly them.
It is realized that it takes about the same time to train a man to fly as it does to build a plane. Therefore we have felt that it would be desirable to keep a small compact force made up of the various fighting elements which could be rapidly expanded in time of necessity and which would1 be available at a moment's notice at any time.
The hon. member asked how we were working with the other forces. We are working in the closest cooperation with both the army and the navy. Hon. members have heard of the winter exercises that are to foe carried on this winter by the army. The air force is cooperating in the dropping of supplies and will work with the army throughout.
The question of a fleet air arm has been raised. At the present time the officers of my department and of the naval department are holding discussions in an effort to work out how they can best integrate the training of those who will be flying in the fleet air arm. I think satisfactory arrangements will be worked out whereby the air force will be responsible for the training on land and the providing of bases and airports for the navy fliers when they are on land, and the navy of course will look after them when they once go to sea.
The hon. member for Yorkton mentioned research and suggested that a greater percentage of these appropriations should be allotted to that work. I would point out

Demobilization-Air Services
that the appropriation asked for is largely for expenditures incurred during the war. It is realized that in peace time we shall have to devote a considerable amount of money to research work. We are doing that in close cooperation with the army and the navy. We have a research and development board on which are representatives of the three services. There will be no overlapping, and the work will be carried on in conjunction with the officers of the three services and of the national research council.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to have a brief word. I think the government is to be congratulated upon having two good ministers for national defence. To look at each of these men you can see that not only have they acted the part, they look the part. Neither of them is overweight, which is in keeping with the slogan of each force that it shall cany no excess baggage.
While the air is not man's natural sphere, the air force has conquered the air. Somebody has said that if the Almighty had expected man to occupy the air he would have been equipped with wings like the birds or angels. Man has shown that he does not need that equipment. The air force does not need anyone to defend its record; the record of the air force stands supreme. They have done a job for which all Canada is grateful.
Because of the great distances in Canada I think the minister would be well advised to have a strong permanent force. Look at the men from whom such a force could be picked. These men have been through the war; they have had a course of training second to none. No doubt it has become a proverb that no dunce could receive his wings in the air force. I commend the minister for trying to build up a permanent air force. Such a force should have its stations located from north to south and from east to west. They should cover the whole country. This brings me to the question I wish to ask.
There should be a permanent station at the head of the lakes, at Port Arthur, Fort William and the Thunder Bay district. Even though we are located at the head of the lakes we are the centre of Canada. We are the great distributing point at the head of the greatest fresh water lake which will be on the great waterway. It is not only the centre of Canada materially, but because of the progressive spirit of those two cities it is going to become the hub of Canada, Therefore we should have an air station.
Again, we are a long distance from any other large centre. Winnipeg is a long distance away to the west, and Toronto and Montreal are a 47696-113$
long distance away to the east. Therefore we think it would be in the best interests of the permanent force to have a station at the lakehead. There we have a well-equipped air field, with splendid runways. It is perhaps the third best airfield in Canada and is on the new Trans-Canada air route. The field is also well equipped with buildings and is surrounded by Christian people, who, I am sure the minister will agree, would be a splendid tonic for the air force. I think I need use no further argument to convince the minister that it would be in the best interests of the Royal Canadian Air Force to have a station at the head of the lakes.

speechtext:
I wish to bring up a
matter which I have raised on two or three different occasions, and if I am not in order in bringing the matter up now I shall have to wait until the civil estimates come up.
I have reference to a number of young Canadians from Ottawa, Toronto and many other large centres who in 1943 enlisted in the British fleet air arm. When I first heard of this in Toronto, where I knew a number of these young men, I brought the matter up in the House of Commons. The present Premier of Nova Scotia was then minister for the naval services. I informed him about these young men being taken right out of the schools-of course, their parents were informed of their enlistment-and almost before anyone could . know about it they were shipped over to England. The minister at that time apparently was not acquainted with what had taken place. That was in 1943. It seemed strange to me how these young rnen, seventeen, eighteen and nineteen years of age, could be taken right out of their school or university in Canada and be sent across the water to join what turned out to be the British fleet air arm.
I am not finding any fault with the British fleet air arm for trying to get these young men, because heaven knows the mother country at that time was going through what no other nation in the world's history had gone through and she needed the bravest of the brave, which aptly describes these young men.
I brought the matter up again in the house last year, in March of 1944. At that time many of these young men had come back to this side of the water and had been sent to train at Pensacola in the United States. After training there they were sent off to the old land. At Pensacola many if not all of these young men made application for transfer to the Canadian service, and they were informed that in due course they would be transferred to the Royal Canadian Air Force. But when they arrived in England a number of them were kept there, while the rest were sent, some to the Indian ocean and some to the Pacific ocean. Those
Demobilization-Air Services

who went to the Indian ocean took part in the campaign waged by the British fleet air arm against the Japanese, and those who went to the Pacific ocean later flew over Tokyo in attacks on Japan from British carriers.
An Ottawa father of one of these young men came to see me yesterday. He is a prominent man in Ottawa who had read of my asking a question about these young men in the house a few days ago, and he told me of his son's flying over Tokyo. Apparently these young men who got as far as the Indian or the Pacific ocean were out of touch with whoever took their applications for transfer . to the Canadian service, which was what they all wanted to do. Those who remained in England and were not sent to the Pacific or the Indian Ocean were transferred to the Canadian service.
What I feel is this. I think all these men should be treated on the same basis. I do not know how many of them there are; but certainly if fifty young men applied at Pensacola for transfer to the Canadian service and later twenty-five of them-I am using arbitrary figures-remained in England where, * because they were in closer touch with the authorities, their applications for transfer to the Canadian service were accepted, while those who were sent to the Indian ocean or to the Pacific and did perhaps a greater service did not have their applications for transfer to the Canadian service accepted, I say that that is wholly unfair. I crossed the floor to speak to the Minister of National Defence for Air personally about this matter when his estimates were first before the house. Perhaps I did not present the case to him very clearly, but on that occasion he told me that the matter was under the control of the minister for the navy. So that I let the matter go until just a few days ago when it was getting near the end of the debate on the army estimates. I then asked the Minister of National Defence about this matter, and he stated that it was not in his department and gave a general reply to my inquiry. I still maintain that it'is wholly unfair that these men who applied during their training at Pensacola for transfer to the Royal Canadian Air Force should not have been accepted for the Canadian service.

The question of the fleet air arm comes entirely under the navy. We have the same minister for both army and navy; I suppose that if the matter was brought up on his army estimates he may have said it was out of place on that occasion; but I shall be glad to take the matter up with him.

Now Canada has some of these ships, and I understand they will probably be getting some Canadians in the fleet air arm of the navy.
I heard the very fine speech which was made by the hon. member for Quebec South, and I agreed very largely if not altogether with what he said. He made a plea that we should not have duplication in air services in this country. I think that is an extremely sound stand to take. We have followed up his suggestions. speechtext: Yes, it is so. I know, because I was out talking in one of the stations, finding out what the score was. Now you want to reduce the ranks to whatever level you see fit. But it is not the rank the boys are worried about; it is the pay. The pay envelope is the only reason a man accepts promotion; he takes it because he can get a little more money. This cheap method is not going to work; the boys are not reacting favourably to it. During the war we had this set-up, that an aeroplane went in the air with, say, a crew of four or eight men, of whom half might be officers and half N.C.O.'s. Every man was a good' man in his individual place. But when they came down the caste system of the permanent force separated them socially. An N.C.O. got "six bits" for his flight and an officer got two dollars. The modern machine has destroyed the caste system; yet it is maintained here because of the class nature of our society. We shall have to do away with that and make it more flexible.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question? The hon. gentleman was in the air force. Did he have a square deal, or did he not, in that force?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I told the committee I had a square deal except when a permanent force man came along.	,

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Yes, I went through it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I am asking you. Put it on the record-that is what I want-whether you had a square deal or not.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
We had also the difference in pay between W.D.'s and men. We stand for equal pay for equal work. These girls, up to the limit of their ability, filled the job in some cases as well as the men did, and yet there was this discrepancy. When I went to the Edmonton manning depot one of the first things we received was a lecture on esprit de corps, and I shall never forget that as long as I live. An officer got up and every quotation on esprit de corps which he gave came from a German textbook. The Joe sitting next to me said, "What's this?" I did not enlighten him. However, the point is this, that we had no textbook; we had nothing to teach the men so that they could develop that spirit. It was right there, apparent in the lecture which this officer gave. We must develop a national philosophy, an esprit de corps that will inspire men who are will-(Mr. Archibald.]
ing to sacrifice themselves. There is too much cynicism going around in this country at the present time. We know that before 1914, before the last war there was a great deal of spirit in this nation, but there was less of it this .time, because the boys had gone through an unemployment period. They did not know any trades and we had to develop trades in a hurry. Men often went out ill trained and now we hear that there are five thousand returned men unemployed at Windsor. The government had better put them to work and keep them at work so that we shall have the skill necessary for the nation in the next war. If they do not, we are doomed.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: During recent months I have had interviews with, and have received letters from, young women with lengthy service who wished to get their release because they had opportunities for civilian employment of a high order. I will give an illustration. A certain young woman served a long time in New York and gave excellent service for nearly four years. Prior to enlisting she was well known in mining circles in British Columbia and had a continent-wide reputation. Her work in connection with the British Columbia mines exhibit at the San Francisco exhibition was of the highest kind. She had experience in mining, prospecting, company organization and so on. She has an opportunity now to return to that employment; and if the minister will refer to the department of mines of British Columbia, or the chamber of mines in Vancouver or in Nelson, he will be told that this young woman is urgently needed to return to that work at this time. I mention that by way of illustration. These young women to whom I have been talking explain to me that in many cases they were doing quite routine work. Most of them belong to the clerks administrative. They are a responsible, reliable type of young women who are anxious to return to civilian employment. My question is this. When does the minister think it will be possible for this type of personnel to secure release?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
That is a difficult question, in that we have the women's division which is- being demobilized in the same way as the men's division, and the members of that division are going out in the same proportion as they are to the total number of men in the service. In the air force we have various trades, and those in some trades that can be spared are being demobilized more rapidly than in other trades where their services are required. At the present time

Demobilization-Air Services
during the period of demobilization there are two trades that are very necessary to the force, clerks administrative and clerks accountant. It will be realized that there is a great deal of clerical work to be done in connection with the demobilization of a large force, with the result that we are not able to let them out as rapidly as some of the other trades. They are being demobilized bn the basis of "first in, first out", and the W.D. referred to, if she has a position to go to and is entitled to preference, can go to the position when the air force can spare her services. But we have to consider the welfare of the service as a whole. We do not wish to slow up demobilization by letting out too many clerks and then having our repatriation centres hlocked because we cannot get the clerical work done in order to have releases put through.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The hon. member for Fort William emphasized the fact that there were two capable ministers on the opposite side. That is a very small percentage, so that we can be generous on, this side of the house. But his motive was to advocate the advantages of having a flying field or station established in his constituency. It would save a lot of time, in case other hon. members on the other side of the house intend to make similar addresses, if the Minister of National Defence for Air would tell us where the five operational stations which he is retaining will be located. That is the first question.
The second is this. He made reference to the close cooperation existing between the Department of National Defence for Naval Services and his own department and said that he did not want to see any unnecessary duplication in the field of flying. Might I ask him whether some liaison exists between the Department of Justice and his own department, because no doubt the Royal Canadian Mounted Police would probably utilize the aeroplane in their operations?
The third question that I would ask him arises from the question I asked on October 4 regarding the early training of prospective officers for the R.C.A.F. Before this war, graduates from the Royal Military College at Kingston were allowed to enter the R.C.A.F. under certain conditions, and students from the universities were also admitted under a certain set of other conditions. They, too, were permitted to enter into the regular R.C.A.F. before the war, and I should like to know what arrangements are being made for the intake of future officers because, if parents are to give their boys, who they hope will follow the R.C.A.F. as a future career, any special form of educational training they
should be advised at the earliest possible opportunity. I would point out that these boys who go through such colleges as the Royal Military College or the Royal Naval College do receive certain not only definite advantages, so far as academic and1 physical training are concerned, but also financial advantages by attending these government-supported colleges. Is it the intention of the R.C.A.F. to start a college of their own? Those are the three questions I should like to have answered.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
As to the first question, I mentioned that we have five operational stations being maintained at the present time. I did not mean that we would have only five operational stations in Canada, or five permanent stations, in our post-war set-up. I have seen the plans that we are working on and I expect that more than five stations will be kept on a permanent basis throughout Canada, but I do not want to give the names at the present time because as yet no definite decision has been reached as to where they will be located, although they-will be spread across Canada, not only on the coasts but inland as well. In addition, we shall have our airports where auxiliary squadrons will be located, and we shall have a training establishment as well. So that we shall have quite a number of stations throughout Canada, considerably more than five. The five to which I referred previously were the last remaining operational stations that had been in service during the war.
In regard to cooperation with the Department of Justice, I have had consultations with the Minister of Justice concerning assistance for the mounted police, and we have given some undertaking as to how we can help them. I do not know yet how far they intend to go in providing flying training for the mounted police, but there is no doubt that they will receive eveTy cooperation on the part of the air force. I am not certain as to whether they intend to set up their own establishment of aircraft, but undoubtedly if they are going to train pilots the R.C.A.F. will be willing to undertake to provide the courses required.
In connection with the training of prospective officers, that again comes under the postwar plan. There have been suggestions from some sources that since we have a military college and a naval college we should have an air force college. Another point of view is that we should have a training school at which men will qualify for commissions as they qualified during the war. That matter is under consideration at the present time. No decision has been reached as yet as to what the terms of service will be or in what way commissions
Demobilization-Air Services

will be granted in the post-war force. Of course those who are signing on for the interim force have the undertaking that if they wish to remain in the permanent force they will be kept on.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Is there any opportunity
for those in the interim force now to prepare for commissioned rank?

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Educational courses are run in the service to qualify men. That has been done all through the war; and men in the ranks who are recommended for commissions are, of course, commissioned in the force.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I should like to speak on
behalf of the airmen who enlisted away back in 1940. I have in mind a boy who did 1,212 hours of flying; who volunteered three times to go overseas and was always turned down because he was said to be an indispensable man. That did not apply to only one man; it applied to many. Now, after five and a half years spent in training these wonderful fliers, these men whom we have read so much about, some of whom helped to save Britain, these men find that when they ask for a job they are told they have no overseas service and so cannot get that job. I think that is very unfair, because these men offered to go overseas. These were the men who enlisted in 1940. When they apply for positions in the government service they are told, "No job can be offered because you are not a veteran with overseas service." These men could not possibly have done any better. They were frozen in their jobs; they had to stay there, and now when they come to re-enter civilian life they are victimized. I do not believe that is fair, that situation should be remedied. The other fellow who got overseas, who perhaps was in Britain all the time and who never put in 1,200 hours flying time, is able to come back and get a job in the civil service. I should like the minister to consider that situation and weigh these cases. A man who enlisted in 1940, who volunteered three times for overseas service and was turned down because he was needed at a station here in the commonwealth training plan, should be given some consideration. I want the minister to look into that.
There is another point. I notice that every hon. member who rises to speak boasts about his constituency. If the hon. member for Fort William ever plans to establish an air station I suggest that he come out to Gimli and see what a real air station looks like.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I know all about it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Can the minister give me any information as to what is likely to happen
{Mr. C. W. G. Gibson.]
at Gimli? Is it to be a permanent station? We have a real, live council there, and their post-war plans will depend upon the-plans of the air force with regard to that station, in connection with housing accommodation, water facilities and different improvements they intend to make.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I understand that Gimli is on the list for use after the war. Just how it will be used I am not prepared to say at the present time, but it is recognized as a valuable airport and it is likely it will be used.
The matter of the civil service preference has given me a good deal of heart-burning, because I realize that a great many members of the air force were kept in this country against their will. They were required here in connection , with the commonwealth air training plan. Many of them who were very anxious to go overseas were forcibly retained in this country to act as instructors. After the last war the civil service preference meant that a person had to land in England before becoming eligible for it. I hope to be successful in having that extended to include those who have flown beyond the territorial waters of Canada, which would take in those flying from our coasts on convoy work and coastal patrol. But I think it will be realized that to extend the preference to all members of the force who served in Canada would create such an enormous class of people who would be entitled to the preference that it would practically remove that benefit in the case of the man who had served overseas.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: Don't you think-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I must draw the attention of the committee to the fact that the question of employment in the civil service does not come under these estimates. It is a question for the Department of the Secretary of State and the Department of Veterans Affairs and should be considered when the estimates of those departments are before the committee. I do not want to be too strict in these matters, but it does seem to me that if we are to make any progress our discussion should be with respect to the estimates before the committee. I would therefore ask hon. members not to discuss the estimates of other departments at the present time.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I want to abide by your ruling, Mr. Chairman.
The last time I spoke in the house I said that I never rise but I am ruled out of order, either one way or another. I do not want to be that way. I want to keep within the rules of the house, just the same as any other body. But does the minister not think that there

Demobilization-Air Services
should be included in that category men who have flown over a thousand hours and who enlisted in 1940, men who were turned down three times before going overseas. They were the men who saved the country, those men who went in 1940 without any compulsion whatsoever.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I was wondering if it might not be possible for us to save time by disposing of the general discussion, and then adhering to the items. It seems to me that within the last while questions have been asked which might more properly be asked under one of these fourteen items. If we proceed in this fashion we are in danger of duplicating our discussions.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
What the hon. member for Wellington South has said is quite true. But he must remember that we are ti-ying to draw from the minister some idea as to the general policy his department is going to follow. We know the war is over, and we want to know now what the future policy is to be.
After all, viewed1 in the light of decades or centuries, this is a new department, and a new function of government. This has come in our time. It is an expensive function, but a very necessary one and, as the hon. member for Trinity said, one which did a great deal to preserve our present civilization.
At the height of the war we did not mind spending money, and we voted it without hindrance. True, we investigated some policies and ideas promulgated with the advent of the Department of National Defence for Air. But it is just as true that we overlooked many features in the conduct of that department which we did not entirely approve. No one knows better than the hon. member for Wellington South, who has just taken his seat, that we saw duplication in all the services which, in ordinary business practice, would not be permitted.
I would ask the minister this evening to let us know his policy in respect of (a) clothing and supplies of a kind suitable for air force, and at the same time for army personnel. I agree that the navy, a force old in tradition and in habit, might not wish to be coupled with the army, although to my mind, in this day if we are to follow good business practice, all departments should look to economy in conducting their affairs, and wherever possible should do their purchasing and their handing out of supplies through one purchasing system. There should be uniformity, instead of keeping up three or four distinct
systems, as we find it at the present time. Therefore I ask why there could not be some coordination in the purchasing of clothing.
.Then, (b) what is the position in connection with diets? Set up within the organization of the air department is a distinct and separate system of diets. This might have been necessary when the war was at its height, and diets for airmen were different from those-of men in the army. But am I not within the judgment of the chamber when I ask the department at this time to give some consideration to coalescing its effort with the effort being made by the army along similar lines?
Then, (c) in connection with housing, the housing the men receive, the hours they are on duty, and the service they are to give; is there not some way in which we might lay down a policy so that there will be more uniformity in that regard, and less of those jealousies we see emanating from men in different cloth, all of whom are serving our country?
Then, (d) what about the men requiring examinations and hospitalization? We know that hospitalization was built up across Canada-not in one unit, oh, no; rather, in four units. The navy had its ideas respecting a system of hospitalization; the army had ideas of its own, and so had the air force. My good friend the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) knows that the old Department of Pensions and National Health had its ideas, too.
Each branch had its own supplies coming from different units, different purchasing agents. Many times those supplies were going to the same destination, and at great expense. When some years ago officials were cross-examined on the point, we received this reply: How would it be possible for a man in blue who was hospitalized to be served by a medical man in khaki? It just was not done! A man in air force uniform could not accept treatment from a man in khaki-and the minister knows that is on the record.
But we were at war in those days. Stress and strain on our country made it necessary for those members who interested themselves in matters of that kind to curb their inclination to criticize, so that we could get on with the war.
I say to the administration: The war is over. We are asking the minister now to recite the policy for his department. This is a good department to begin with, because it is new. In the name of economy let him coalesce, as best he can, the different features of cost which he believes necessary, in order that he might have a first-class Department

Demobilization-Air Services

of National Defence for Air, which would work alongside and in harmony with other branches of national defence.
With all due respect to the hon. member for Wellington South, this is a time when the minister should rise in his place and recite to Canada to-night what the general policy of his department is to be. I agree with what was said a few minutes ago by the hon. member for Davenport. The previous minister recited a policy of a kind which would coalesce the efforts of the different branches of national defence. Yea, Mr. Chairman, he went so far as to originate a committee composed of different units of the armed services, to sit in month by month for the purpose of finding where economies could be effected. While we have asked across the floor of the house for the minutes of that committee, to my knowledge they have never yet been tabled.
The minister of that day felt that something of that kind should be done. The new minister has no doubt studied what has happened in the last three or four years, and in his studies he must have come across that idea which was put forward by his predecessor. Then, too, he must have some ideas of his own which would be in the general interest of Canada, and particularly when the country is no longer at war.
I am not of opinion that we should carry-on a tremendous organization which would keep active all those features ancillary to the actual service in war time, but I am strongly of the opinion of the hon. member for York-ton who stated a few minutes ago that the developments and advancements which are being made should be part and parcel and one of the first responsibilities of the Minister of National Defence for Air. That is aside from the question of economy which I was trying to emphasize. Spend all the money necessary for research and keeping right up to the last minute, but in the business administration and the actual work within the department let us have some coalescing with the other departments of national defence and let us show some signs of real economy now that the war is over.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I am glad to reply to those remarks because I feel thg.t a definite effort has been made to prevent overlapping in the work of the various departments. The hon. member for Danforth has suggested that one system should be adopted in providing clothing and supplies. Throughout the war the procurement of clothing and supplies has been done by one department, the Department of Munitions and Supply. When any one of the forces had any require-
ments, they made out their list and the purchasing was done by that department. There was no competition between the army and navy and air force for the supplies which were required and which might be in short supply.
The same thing is true in connection with diet and food. Food for the air force is supplied by the army service corps. I quite agree that our flyers overseas did receive some special food. For example, they had an additional supply of milk, and we went to some expense to provide that for those who were engaged in aircrew duties. But the basic food supplies were supplied to the air force by the army service corps.
The same thing applies to hospitalization and medical supplies. Medical supplies are provided to air force hospitals by the army medical corps. These supplies are bought in bulk and distributed in that way. I am prepared to admit that in the early days of the war when hospitals had to be provided at a rapid rate, the air force secured buildings and established their own hospitals. These have now come under the general control, and no hospital is built or planned for until it has been approved by the wartime committee on hospitalization. This is a government committee which plans all hospital requirements in this country and coordinates the efforts of all departments in the field of hospitalization.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I hope the
minister will check that statement with regard to hospitalization with his colleague who is sitting beside him. He knows that they impinge on the old pensions and national health, now veterans affairs, rather than on the army. There are two distinct set-ups.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I shall be glad to check that.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Neither one
knows what the other is doing. They arc both trying to do the same thing. That is the condition right here within rifle range of this building, and that is just one example.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
This is a matter we discussed before. I do not want to get the committee confused in what was voted at the last session and what was actu-. ally granted. While it is included in the total amount required, it is not included in the amount we are asking the committee to vote at this time.	In my estimates the
requirements for the total year are $598,487,116.	We have already been granted
$325,985,039, which means there is an additional amount of $272,502,077 required, which we are asking the committee to pass.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
There are a couple of questions I should like to ask, and since I cannot find an appropriate item under which to ask them, I am asking them now. Can the minister give us some information about the disposition of the airports at Dauphin? There are two fine airports there, No. 10 and No. 7. I should like to refer to sessional paper 142B which contains the answers to some questions I asked. The first question was:
What decision has been reached as to the retention or disposal of (a) the main aerodrome at Dauphin, Manitoba?
That was No. 10 service flying school. The answer given was this:
This unit, formerly No. 10 service flying training school, is now being used to store reserve equipment and will be required indefinitely by the R.C.A.F. At - such time as the unit becomes surplus the aerodrome and buildings will be referred to the Department of Transport.
I should like to know if that service flying training school is still being used for the 47696-114J	'
storage of reserve equipment or whether it has been transferred to the Department of Transport.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I am informed that we are still using that for the storage of reserve equipment. When it is needed no longer it will be turned over' to Transport for whatever use they may decide to make of it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
My next question was as to No. 7 bombing and gunnery school at Paulson, Manitoba, and the answer was:
Certain facilities at this school, which disbanded on 15th September, 1945, will be retained for R.C.A.F. use. The remainder will be referred to Department of Transport.
I should like to know what these "certain facilities" are and how long it is intended to use them for this purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: I shall be glad to give that information to my hon. friend later.	,

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: What is being done or is proposed to be done about the photographic division of the air force? I know there have been some flights for mapping during the past summer. Is that to be continued, and, if so, on what scale? Is the whole country to be photographed from the air and mapped? I ask this question because a chap who was attached to No. 7 photographic wing came to see me about two weeks ago and told me that he in'eompany with a considerable number of other airmen, mostly N.C.O.'s, have been sitting around for the last month or so more or less twiddling their thumbs, and in the meantime trying without success to get their release from the air force. Are these men being kept on for some particular purpose? If not, is the establishment to be reduced? According to my information a considerable number of these men think that the chief reason for their being kept on is to provide a good excuse for the continuance of jobs for certain high-ranking officers, which is a poor spirit on the part of men in any service.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
The air
force have had two photo squadrons up to the present. One of them has been engaged in doing work for the Department of Mines and Resources. During the past summer we have photographed in the neighbourhood of 200,000 square miles of this country. This means that a great deal of work will still have to be done in the station developing the negatives and preparing the maps for them, so that there should be a good deal of work at headquarters of the photo squadrons. It is not intended
Demobilization-Air Services

to retain both squadrons in the post-war setup ; we shall have only one. It is possible that some of the work that we have been doing for other departments will have to be done by civilian companies.
I am glad that my hon. friend has brought up the question of dissatisfaction at wing headquarters because I have heard rumours of it myself, that the men felt they were being held there when they should be allowed to get out. I had a report made on the establishment that was fairly satisfactory, but I am having another report made to find out if the men are being demobilized in proper rotation and if any men are being retained whose services are not required. I am glad, I say, that my hon. friend has raised the question because, if in any station the men have the feeling that they are not being fairly dealt with, I want to know about it and I want to investigate it.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
On what scale will this
aerial mapping be done in the future? How many square miles are likely to be mapped in a year?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It is rather difficult for me to say. The work is planned by the Department of Mines and Resources, which requests us to do certain work. We have done work not only for that department but sometimes for provincial governments. Our own squadron will be doing work of a service nature from now on. I would not be prepared to say how many square miles of mapping will be done in a season.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext: It is a valuable service and I was hoping that it would be continued on a reasonably large scale.

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Has the minister's attention
been drawn to a statement which received wide publicity a short time ago which was made by the head of Trans-Canada Air Lines to the effect that he found R.C.A.E. pilots unsatisfactory in some respects in civil operations? Has the minister had any member of his staff investigate this statement? It seems to me absurd to say that men who have flown without all the aids that civilian pilots have had during the war prove unsatisfactory for ordinary air line operation.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
I did see the remarks that were made by an officer of Trans-Canada Air Lines and I considered them unfortunate, but I have hesitated to make reply to them because often more harm can be done than good accomplished by starting a controversy between two government departments. I want our men to have the feeling when they come out that they will have an

opportunity to join Trans-Canada Air Lines, and I should not like to have any bad feeling existing between the two organizations.
In fairness to our own pilots I should like to put on the record what our men have -accomplished in the way of transport work.
The R.C.A.F.'s transatlantic transport squadron's record of 450 transatlantic crossings from January 1, 1944, to October 31, 1945, with but two fatal accidents one of these on take-off, will stand favourable comparison with any other transatlantic transport operations during a similar period.
The record of 164 squadron, flying a schedule on the east coast of Canada,'Newfoundland and Labrador, operating often in some of the foulest weather to be found on the north American continent, is even more impressive. A typical year, 1944, saw this squadron move 25,980 passengers, a total payload of 12,300,000 pounds over an air mile distance of 2,670,000. The squadron has never had a fatal accident and has never lost an aircraft since it was organized in 1943.
The record of 165 squadron, operating on the west coast, with the added hazard of mountain flying, is also impressive. That squadron has had but one fatal accident since it was organized in 1943. In 1944 the squadron moved 23,573 passengers a total payload of
9,618,000	pounds over an air-mile distance of
1,290,000.
The ferry wing of R.C.A.F. transport, in no small measure was responsible for the success of the gigantic British commonwealth air training plan, in 1944 delivered 9,152 planes in 55,365 flying hours for a total air-mile distance of 6,718,500.
It is not the intention of the R.CA.F. to allow the immeasurable experience gained during the war to be wasted. This experience came from one schedule that had its origin at Roekcliffe and its termination at Cairo, with a feeder service to continental Europe, Gibraltar, North Africa and Italy; from another schedule on the east coast of Canada, Newfoundland and Labrador; and from another that covered the entire west coast and what is now known as the northwest staging route.
That is a record of which the Royal Canadian Air Force can well be proud:

maintopic: DEPARTMENT OF NATIONAL DEFENCE FOR AIR
speechtext:
Further to what the hon. member for Calgary East had to say about No. 7 photographic wing, my information is that they were not only not busy but they were operating in two shifts, a night shift and a day shift, and my further information is that this was done to prevent too much congestion during the day time.

Would the minister make a statement or give his views on the suggestion I advanced when the naval estimates were under consideration and this item was being discussed, as to the possibility of establishing a joint signals school for the three services? As I pointed out at that time, we are being asked to vote under this item for signals and wireless equipment some $40,000,000 for the three services, and in my view a substantial saving could be achieved in the
future if the resources of the services were pooled, particularly for the basic training stages. Would the minister indicate his view as to that suggestion?

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I did not hear my hon. friend make that suggestion, but it is one that might very well be explored. Of course there would be differences in the equipment used in the air force, the army and the navy. Was the suggestion that the three services would combine?

Yes, so that the equipment used in the initial training of signallers in the three services might be pooled. I can quite well understand that later on specialized training would require different types of equipment; but even that training I should think might be carried on in three different branches of the same school instead of there being three entirely separate schools and three separate lots of equipment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Defence for Air
speechtext: I am not an expert on signalling, and I would not want to express my own opinion as to whether or not that would be feasible, but certainly it is a suggestion that should be explored. Probably anyone who was an expert on signalling work would be able to give an opinion, but I can assure my hon. friend that I shall have the suggestion looked into.

One other advantage which might be suggested in support of that contention is that which would follow in the standardization of signal practice. As many hon. members will recall, it was found during this war that the signal practice and procedure in the three services was entirely different. This was responsible for a great deal of delay, and eventually it was found necessary more or less to standardize it. I suggest that this would automatically follow the founding of a joint school.
